headings.title: Introduction and Cultural Context of Self-Medication in Nigeria
headings.content: Self-medication involves obtaining and consuming pharmaceutical products without a certified medical prescription. In the Nigerian context, this practice is deeply rooted in socio-economic factors. Long queues in public hospitals, the high cost of formal consultations, and the easy accessibility of medications in open-air drug markets, roadside stalls, and local chemist shops drive many citizens to diagnose themselves. Patent medicine vendors often act as primary healthcare providers despite lacking formal clinical training. While this approach offers temporary convenience, it exposes individuals to severe health hazards due to inappropriate drug selection and incorrect dosages.

headings.title: Commonly Misused Over-the-Counter Substances
headings.content: Certain medications are frequently purchased and ingested without professional guidance, leading to widespread abuse. Analgesics, particularly paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen, top the list for frequent misuse. Antimalarials are also heavily self-administered based on perceived symptoms of fever rather than confirmatory diagnostic tests like malaria rapid diagnostics. Additionally, cough syrups containing codeine and various vitamin supplements are consumed excessively, often exceeding recommended daily allowances and placing undue stress on excretory organs.

headings.title: Physiological Risks and Adverse Drug Reactions
headings.content: Unsupervised drug consumption directly threatens vital organ systems. Hepatic and renal tissues bear the brunt of this burden because the liver metabolizes xenobiotics while the kidneys filter and excrete them. Excessive intake of paracetamol rapidly depletes glutathione stores in the liver, leading to acute hepatic necrosis. Similarly, chronic ingestion of strong painkillers compromises renal perfusion, precipitating chronic kidney disease. Gastrointestinal bleeding is another frequent complication arising from the irritation of the gastric mucosa by unprescribed non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

headings.title: The Growing Threat of Antimicrobial Resistance
headings.content: Indiscriminate use of antibiotics and antimalarials accelerates the development of resistant pathogen strains. When patients take partial doses or stop medications prematurely because symptoms subside, surviving microbes undergo selective pressure. These stronger microorganisms mutate and multiply, rendering standard pharmaceutical treatments ineffective. Consequently, common infections that were once easily treated now linger, requiring expensive, highly toxic reserve drugs and increasing hospital admission rates across healthcare facilities.

headings.title: Masking of Underlying Serious Medical Conditions
headings.content: Self-medication frequently provides a false sense of security by suppressing vital warning signs of critical diseases. A patient experiencing persistent abdominal pain may rely on antacids or analgesics, temporarily easing discomfort while an underlying peptic ulcer perforates or appendicitis progresses toward rupture. Similarly, using over-the-counter cough mixtures can delay the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis or early-stage lung malignancies. This delay in seeking professional medical evaluation often results in late-stage disease presentation where therapeutic interventions yield poor outcomes.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Patient Education Strategies
headings.content:
- **Assessment**: Conduct thorough medication histories during patient intake to identify unsupervised drug use.
- **Education**: Counsel patients on the dangers of sharing prescriptions and purchasing drugs from informal vendors.
- **Advocacy**: Promote strict adherence to prescribed treatment regimens and emphasize completing full antibiotic courses.
- **Collaboration**: Work with community health teams to raise public awareness regarding safe medication practices.
